cl_xc_mindset_before.q: Does how I feel beforehand change how a psychedelic trip goes?
cl_xc_mindset_before.short: Feeling calm and ready beforehand went with easier trips; feeling anxious went with more anxiety.
cl_xc_mindset_before.but: These are links: no study we read changed how people felt beforehand to test it.
how: About 650 people planning their own trip answered surveys; about 200 answered enough to be counted. Those who felt calm, open and ready the day before said the trip was less hard.
In lab studies of LSD, feeling anxious before the dose went with more anxiety. Feeling well went with stronger effects overall, not easier ones.
Bigger links come from people remembering their mood afterwards, and memories can be coloured by how the trip went.
Clinical trials prepare people with meetings and advice. But a review of 25 trials found none that compared different ways of preparing.

cl_xc_setting_support.q: Do the place and the people around me affect a trip?
cl_xc_setting_support.short: In surveys, feeling safe and supported went with fewer difficult moments, by small amounts.
cl_xc_setting_support.but: People rated this looking back; the one study that asked beforehand found only a weak link.
how: In a study that asked the day before, feeling good about the place and people went with slightly easier trips, but the link was weak and could be chance.
Among almost 7,000 people who drank ayahuasca, those who felt safer and better supported at the ceremony reported a little less fear than others.
In a US survey, people who blamed a lack of support for their hardest trip said it was harder than people who did not.

No study we read put people in different places, or with different people, on purpose to compare them. A review of 25 clinical trials found none either, and the trials set up their rooms and staff in very different ways.

cl_xc_music.q: Does music change how a psychedelic session goes?
cl_xc_music.short: Patients said music shaped their sessions; two kinds of music made no clear difference.
cl_xc_music.but: None of the studies we read compared music with silence, and the trial of two kinds of music had only 10 people.
how: 19 patients with hard-to-treat depression took psilocybin in a clinic with the same music. Almost all said it helped at times; about half said it sometimes made things harder.
Patients who spoke more warmly about the music had a bigger drop in depression a week later. But both were measured at the same time.

In a trial of 10 people trying to quit smoking, each had one session with classical music and one with gongs and singing bowls, in random order. How mystical or hard the sessions felt did not clearly differ.
In a US survey, people who linked their hardest time to the music did not rate it as harder than others did.

cl_ket_music.q: Does music change how a ketamine session goes?
cl_ket_music.short: In one trial, the top blood pressure number rose less with music. How it feels is unknown.
cl_ket_music.but: Just one small trial of 32 patients in hospital, and it reported only blood pressure.
how: 32 patients with hard-to-treat depression had a course of up to six ketamine drips in hospital. Some were picked at random to hear music during each drip; the rest heard none.
With music, the top blood pressure number rose about 7 points less during each drip.
The trial has not yet reported how the sessions felt or whether depression improved.
Earlier, a review found 14 studies of music with ketamine, mostly with other medicines during surgery or tests. It found no study comparing music with no music in ketamine treatment for depression.
